text: Today we are looking at duplicate execution in a stateful concurrent system. The key problem is not that a worker runs once and fails. It is that the same operation can run again and quietly violate the invariant that was supposed to hold.

Start with the chain: at-least-once delivery creates pressure, that pressure leads to double processing, and double processing can inflate side effects. Once you name the invariant, the design response becomes a question of evidence and control.

Here the pressure becomes concrete. Worker A receives the event, does the work, and then the acknowledgement is lost. The queue redelivers the same event to Worker B, and the side effect happens twice. That is what at-least-once delivery really means in practice.

The second view is the guard path. A worker claims the event, checks the idempotency store, and records the transition in the audit log before moving forward. The point is to make repeat delivery observable instead of destructive, but that only works if the ordering is durable.

This is the failure in concrete terms: Worker A ships order-42, crashes before the acknowledgement, and Worker B ships order-42 again. The happy path still looked fine, which is why the baseline creates false confidence. A reviewer should be able to reconstruct the duplicate from delivery IDs, operation IDs, and crash and redelivery logs.

The second failure view explains the false confidence directly. A sequential test can pass once, but real pressure exposes duplicate execution and violates the invariant. The mistake is assuming one clean run proves the system can tolerate repetition.

So the next question is what protects the invariant. An idempotency key, a durable completion record, or another guarded transition lets the handler decide once and avoid inflating the external effect. The fix improves safety, but it also adds storage, state modeling, and more handler logic.

The retry-safe pattern makes the mechanism explicit: claim once, reject repeated claims, perform the side effect, and record completion durably before the retry can re-enter. If the worker succeeds but the acknowledgement is lost, the retry path still has to be safe. The fix protects the invariant, but it does not erase the operational trade-offs.

At this point the trade-off table becomes the design argument. A simple baseline is easy to explain but hides timing pressure; a guarded transition protects the invariant directly; explicit coordination makes ordering visible; and an idempotent design is often the best fit for queues and async workers. For A3, show the failing scenario, the corrected run, structured logs with IDs, and a short defense of the remaining risk.
